summary: A summary from the Network Information Center's viewpoint of what was decided at the February 23, 1973 Network Mail Meeting at SRI-ARC. The main outcome was adding a new FTP mail command with fields such as TO, FROM, AUTHOR and TITLE, where recipients use a user@host form. It points to RFC 475 for a fuller summary.

plainLanguage.summary: Notes from a meeting about sending letters between computers, listing what the letters should say about who sent them and who gets them.

subtitle: Summary of conclusions from the February 1973 Network Mail meeting at SRI-ARC

tldr.problem: The network community needed a standard way to send mail between computers, with clear addressing, sender identification, and delivery tracking.
tldr.mechanism: A meeting at SRI-ARC in February 1973 defined a new FTP mail command with subcommands for TO, FROM, AUTHOR, TITLE, TYPE, and others, standardizing the format as user@host and establishing how the NIC would track mail.
tldr.outcome: This meeting output the conceptual foundation for network mail, which evolved into email standards and practices still in use today.

today: RFC 469 records a pivotal moment in email history. The user@host addressing format became the standard for SMTP email and remains universal today. The FTP-based mail concept evolved into separate protocols (SMTP, POP, IMAP), but the fundamental concepts of addressing, FROM, TO, and TITLE fields persist in modern email.

sections.title: The Network Mail Meeting
sections.content: Michael Kudlick of SRI-ARC summarized the conclusions from the Network Mail Meeting held on February 23, 1973 at SRI-ARC. The meeting brought together key figures in network protocol development to reach consensus on how the ARPANET should handle electronic mail. Kudlick's summary, while brief from the NIC viewpoint, aligned with a more comprehensive summary by Abhay Bhushan (RFC 475). The meeting followed background discussions (RFC 453) and preceded the NIC's detailed requirements (RFC 479).
sections.plainLanguage: Network engineers met to decide how to send mail between computers, and the NIC took notes on what they decided.

sections.title: The FTP Mail Command
sections.content: The meeting decided to implement new FTP mail capabilities through a mail command with several subcommands. The TO field explicitly allowed multiple recipients using a standard syntax: user@host. The FROM field provided a return address for undeliverable mail notifications and clear sender identification. The AUTHOR field listed one or more authors of the mail. The TITLE field contained the subject, terminated by period and carriage return. The TYPE subcommand classified mail as long, urgent, or ordinary, letting recipient hosts decide storage strategy. The TEXT subcommand carried the message itself, while FILE and CITATION provided ways to reference external documents instead of sending full text.
sections.plainLanguage: The new mail system needed fields saying who it is to, who it is from, who wrote it, what it is about, and what to do with it.

sections.title: Addressing and the NIC Role
sections.content: The standard address format user@host became the fundamental addressing scheme. The NIC would maintain identification files mapping from NIC idents or user last names to these standard addresses. For TIP users without a direct host connection, some hosts would be designated as home sites where accounts could be created for sending and receiving mail. The NIC would offer a translation service, available for individual lookups or used automatically when the NIC served as an intermediate delivery point. The NIC could also record mail in its journal with accession numbers for future reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The NIC would keep a directory of who is at which computer so people could find each other by name.

sections.title: Delivery and Recording
sections.content: Mail delivery costs were borne by the sender's host for transmission and the recipient's host for reception and storage. An optional ACKNOWLEDGEMENT field could request notification of delivery or failure. Recorded mail would get a pre-assigned NIC accession number for permanent cataloging and searching. The meeting decided that accession numbers would be obtained from the NIC as needed, though local assignment might later prevent the NIC from becoming a bottleneck. Discussion also noted that recorded documents could eventually reside anywhere on the network, provided there was a central index at the NIC.
sections.plainLanguage: When mail was delivered, either side could ask for a message saying it got there. Important mail could be saved at the NIC and looked up by number.
